title: 2 AM, Ramyeon
description:
The communal kitchen of the goshiwon. 2 AM.

I came out to open the fridge and found Hyunsu already there.

Four years into his Grade 9 civil service exams. Every time I'd seen him before, he had earphones in with a lecture playing — but tonight, he'd just opened a packet of ramyeon and was staring out the window. As {name} waited for the water to boil, he asked, "Not studying today?"

Hyunsu turned. His eyes were a little red.

"...What about you, hyung? Do you think that 3 billion actually going to happen?"

choices.text: "Of course. What's the alternative?" — with conviction
choices.result_text:
"I guess that's enough then." Hyunsu started eating his ramyeon again — like he'd confirmed something.

That night, they both ate in silence. The only sound in the kitchen was the hum of the refrigerator.

choices.text: "I don't know. But if I don't try, it's definitely not happening."
choices.result_text:
Hyunsu smiled. "That's somehow scarier to hear."

A short silence. A car passed outside. The ramyeon had gone soggy, but neither of them touched it.

choices.text: "What about you? Do you think you'll make it?" — turning it back on him
choices.result_text:
Hyunsu was quiet for a while. "...I don't know. And that's what scares me most."

They ate ramyeon together without another word. It was a strangely comfortable silence.

title: The Halfway Mark
description:
Two and a half years since arriving in Seoul. Half of the 240 weeks had passed.

A few days ago, beneath Gangnam's lights, {name} had asked why this road mattered. Tonight, the actual balance and the remaining 120 weeks went beside that answer.

The target and current assets went into the phone calculator. It returned the amount that had to be earned and grown each week.

At the beginning, three billion won had been too abstract to feel heavy. After half the run, it contained people left behind, calls answered, and nights without sleep.

It was not mathematically impossible. But at the present speed, the second half would demand a different price than the first.

choices.text: Closed the calculator, opened another tab.
choices.result_text:
Excitement overtook the fear. Playing it safe now would mean regret later.

Lucky to not have lost anything so far — but now the real game begins.

choices.text: Set the phone down. Just today, nothing more.
choices.result_text:
He hasn't quit yet. That's the proof.

This game isn't only won by the fastest. It's also won by the ones who last.

choices.text: Took out a blank page and started over.
choices.result_text:
Better to be right than fast — that was the lesson.

He went back through each decision he'd made. There were things that needed adjustment. They started to become visible.

title: Sangchul Off Guard
description:
Sangchul's office. We'd stayed late reviewing contract documents.

He stepped away to take a call. Ten minutes. Fifteen.

When he returned, he didn't look like himself. He opened the papers without a word — then suddenly said it.

"That was my son. He wants to drop out of university."

He said it without being asked. "I can't tell if he doesn't want to study, or if he just hates everything right now. Honestly, I don't know."

He'd never said anything like this before.

description_if_known.sangchul_truth_known:
Sangchul came back from the call looking different.

"That was my son. He wants to drop out."

Minjun listened.
He used to think bad people only did bad things.
Sangchul wasn't like that.
This worry — it was real.
And that was the hardest part to hold.

choices.text: "That must be hard." — quiet empathy
choices.result_text:
Sangchul paused, then opened the documents again. "What can you do. It's just life."

After that, {name} saw him a little differently. Even under thirty years of experience, there were things like this.

choices.text: "What did you do, back then?" — curious
choices.result_text:
"Me? I just kept going." He said it looking out the window. "You see something when you keep going. Easy to say now, looking back."

A brief silence fell. Thirty years seemed to live inside it.

choices.text: "What does your son want to do?" — steering toward the son
choices.result_text:
"That's the problem — he doesn't know." Sangchul said.

It sounded like something that applied to {name} too — and he couldn't find a word to say.

title: The Manager's Words
description:
4 PM. The manager called {name} in.

"You seem a little unfocused lately."

{name} had checked a stock app during the morning meeting. Just for a second, or so he thought.

The manager didn't bring it up directly. Just asked, "How are things? Work isn't too much, is it?"

He needed the paycheck here. And he needed to make money over there.
Was it actually possible to do both at the same time?

choices.text: "Sorry. I'll get my head straight." — commit to the job
choices.result_text:
The manager nodded and sent him back. On the way to his desk, {name} turned off notifications from the stock app.

Whether this was the right call, or just another missed opportunity — he wouldn't know until the end of the day.

choices.text: Come clean — "I've been studying something on my own."
choices.result_text:
The manager's expression shifted. "Oh really? What kind of studying?"

The conversation went longer than expected. Turns out the manager was also interested in stocks. An unexpected turn. Whether this would help or come back to bite him was still unknown.

choices.text: "I've just been a little tired. I'll be more careful." — deflect
choices.result_text:
The manager let him go with an unreadable expression. {name} sat back down and slipped his phone into the desk drawer.

How long could this double life continue? He pushed that answer to tomorrow.

title: Old Classmate
description:
At lunch, an old laugh met {name} as soon as he opened the restaurant door. A face from his high-school class. Back then they had worn the same uniform and waited for the same final bell. He remembered them starting from the same line.

His classmate sat among colleagues in a crisp suit, choosing dishes and calling the server with the ease of someone who belonged. {name} held a meal ticket for one.

Their eyes met. The laughter at the other table stopped half a beat late. In the clink of a spoon against a bowl, both men calculated whether to acknowledge each other.

choices.text: Walk over warmly — "Hey, long time no see."
choices.result_text:
"Hey. Long time no see."

His classmate stood at once and shook his hand. "What are you doing these days?" As {name} answered, the man's eyes flicked toward his employee badge and back. "I see. That's great." The response was quick and impeccably polite.

He returned to his colleagues, and their laughter soon resumed. A thin skin formed over the cooling soup in front of {name}. He could not tell which phrase had held less: "long time no see" or "that's great."

choices.text: Pretend not to see him — find a corner seat
choices.result_text:
{name} chose a corner seat and turned his back. Each time the laughter rose across the room, his spoon paused. The stainless-steel cup held a tiny, warped reflection of the other table.

He left half his meal and stood. No one called his name on the walk to the register.

Outside, the sunlight was harsh. Even after the restaurant door closed, he could not decide whether pretending not to see had been a choice or an escape.

choices.text: Go over and have an honest conversation
choices.result_text:
After the colleagues left, the two men stayed for another coffee. His classmate spoke of late nights, loans, and the sleep that had stopped coming. His voice was lower than the laughter had sounded from across the room.

{name} offered some of his own story, though not all of it. They laughed once without deciding who had built the better life.

Outside the restaurant, his classmate said, "We're both still on the way, aren't we?" Perhaps even the memory of a shared starting line had never been entirely true.

title: Fifty Million
description:
{name} turned the calculator off, then on again. The figure remained: 50,000,000 won. Its eight digits looked too bright in the room.

Three billion won was still far away; every calculation made the remaining distance more exact. Yet he had begun with 500,000 won, a balance that once made rent frightening. It had grown a hundredfold, carrying luck, endurance, and several choices he could never make the same way again.

He covered the number with one finger, then revealed it. For the first time, possibility looked less like a feeling than evidence. The refrigerator sounded exactly as it had yesterday.

choices.text: Tell no one. Walk to the convenience store and buy something expensive.
choices.result_text:
Telling anyone would mean explaining only the number. {name} pocketed his phone and went down to the convenience store. He chose the 5,000-won ice cream he usually passed over.

Back home, cold mist clung to his fingers as he opened it. The first bite was too sweet. From the second, it tasted like ordinary ice cream.

He liked that no one knew what he was celebrating. Long after it was gone, the wooden stick remained in his hand.

choices.text: Call his father.
choices.result_text:
Even after calling, {name} did not give the amount. "Things have been going pretty well lately."

His father was quiet for a moment. "That's good. I'm glad." He offered neither congratulations nor warnings. Instead he asked whether {name} had eaten.

After the call, the calculator showed the same figure. Somehow, it felt a little less like a number he held alone.

choices.text: Set the next target immediately — 500 million.
choices.result_text:
On paper, {name} wrote 500,000 won, 50 million won, then 500 million won. The next box held 3 billion won. Arrows between them made a staircase.

Instead of marking 50 million as a victory, he underlined it and began calculating the next step. The pleasure had nowhere to linger.

An impossible wall had divided into several ledges. At the same time, he could finally see the full height left to climb.

title: Hyunsu's New Path
description:
After eleven that night, Hyunsu called.

"Hyung, I'm leaving the goshiwon."

He had boxed up his exam books. By day he would attend an accounting career course; in the evening he would help enter ledgers at a small tax accountant's office. A keyboard clicked beyond the phone, followed by a printer feeding out a page.

The timetable that had ruled four years of his life was gone. For the first time, though, tomorrow had entered his voice.

"I don't know if I'll be good at it. But this time, I chose it."

choices.text: "Good. If you chose it, give it a real try." — encourage him
choices.result_text:
Hyunsu let out a short breath on the other end, almost a laugh.

"You take care too, hyung. Not only when things go well."

After the call, {name} held the dark screen a while. Two people who had met in the same goshiwon now had different tomorrows.

choices.text: "Do you have anything in mind?" — curious
choices.result_text:
"Accounting. It was my major, remember?" Hyunsu said. "I thought it only existed on my diploma. I'm going to try using it again."

It was not strange. It was the first time Hyunsu had spoken about himself in the future tense. {name} listened longer to the keyboard beyond the phone.

choices.text: Offer no advice. Listen to the end.
choices.result_text:
Hyunsu slowly described the career course and tax accountant's office he had found. {name} did not interrupt with an answer.

Before hanging up, Hyunsu said, "Saying it out loud makes it feel real."

Sometimes listening was more exact than pushing someone forward.

title: The Salary Ceiling
description:
The day after Sangchul said they were alike, {name} stayed alone in an office familiar enough that he knew which drawers stuck and could identify his manager by his footsteps.

He spread out his payslip and opened the calculator. He subtracted rent and living costs from his take-home pay, then added optimistic promotions and raises. How long would this salary take to become 3 billion won? The answer did not change. This line could not reach the target.

His father had drawn a salary all his life. Sangchul had said {name} knew what to discard in order to move fast. Fluorescent lights hummed behind the figures. Unable to switch off the calculator, {name} saw with precision that diligence, too, could have a ceiling.

choices.text: Turned off the stock app's alerts.
choices.result_text:
{name} silenced the stock app and laid the phone facedown. During work hours he would protect the salary; after work, he would grow another possibility. The company was not the goal. It was the base that supplied capital.

The next morning he arrived early and finished every assigned task. No one knew he opened a different ledger each night.

He had chosen to hold two lives at once. He did not yet know which hand would loosen first.

choices.text: Opened a job-search site on the way home.
choices.result_text:
On the subway home, {name} opened a job-search site. The higher he set the salary filter, the fewer postings remained and the longer their required experience became. At least the calculation was clear: his current pay would not be enough.

He saved three listings. He did not know which field to enter, or whether its rules would truly be different.

His employee badge swayed in the train-door reflection. It was not the face of someone who had decided to leave, but of someone who had begun looking for somewhere to go.

choices.text: Closed the calculator. He had known this from the start.
choices.result_text:
{name} turned the calculator facedown. He had never planned to reach the goal on salary alone. This was not a notice of failure, he told himself, merely confirmation of the salary's role.

Pay would keep his life standing. The remaining hours would build something else. He woke the work monitor again.

Its light erased the ceiling he had just seen. He knew that disappearing was not the same as being gone.

title: Leaving the Goshiwon
description:
There was no need for a moving truck. Papers bearing the new address sat inside his laptop bag, and the key he had been given was in his pocket. His clothes and books filled two boxes. There was no room left to choose. Today's work was to empty this address and carry the boxes to the new one.

Carrying them one at a time, {name} made a final trip down the goshiwon hallway: peeling wallpaper, the shared refrigerator's motor, detergent mingled with instant ramyeon. A faint light still slipped beneath the lit room next door.

The manager took the goshiwon key at the foot of the stairs. As one small piece of metal left his palm, the new key pressed against his thigh.

"Live well." Behind those words, the door that had been his closed quietly.

choices.text: "Thank you for everything." Keep it brief, and leave.
choices.result_text:
"Thank you for everything."

{name} carried the boxes downstairs, their corners pressing into his forearms as the fluorescent light broke and returned at every landing.

When the entrance shut behind him, exhaust and wet asphalt rushed in. It did not smell good, but there was no ceiling above it.

He checked the papers bearing the new address and shifted the boxes in his arms. He never looked back, but the sound of the automatic door followed him all the way to the bus stop.

choices.text: Knock on the lit neighboring door before leaving.
choices.result_text:
The neighbor who opened the door after a long pause was Hyunsu. One earbud was still in, his eyes bloodshot; a lecture kept playing inside the tiny room.

"Hyung, you're really leaving?"
"Yeah. The boxes are packed. I'm leaving today."

Hyunsu looked at the boxes, then at {name}. "Call me when things work out. No, even if they don't." Embarrassed by his own sincerity, he fiddled with the earbud cord.

The lecture resumed as {name} went downstairs. The new key struck the railing once inside his pocket. The farewell stayed clear even after the door closed.

choices.text: Stop at the end of the hallway. Think about the time spent here.
choices.result_text:
At the end of the hall, {name} stopped and counted the months: the first night he cried, dawns spent heating ramyeon water in the shared kitchen, mornings spent reopening the balance in his banking app. They were not times he could honestly call good.

The wallpaper had peeled, the room had been narrow, and summer brought its own smell. Memory did not preserve that time by its conditions alone.

He touched the handle of what had been his room, then checked that the papers for the new address inside his laptop bag had not folded. When he lifted the boxes and walked toward the address already written there, the hallway looked longer than it had a moment before.

description_if_known.wants_out_of_gosiwon:
There was no need for a moving truck. Clothes, a laptop, and a few books filled two boxes. Carrying them one at a time, {name} made a final trip down the goshiwon hallway.

Peeling wallpaper. The shared refrigerator's motor. Detergent mingled with instant ramyeon. Light still spilled from beneath the lit room next door.

When the manager took his key, a small piece of metal vanished from his palm. "Live well."

Only after mastering thirty months of life here had he admitted, for the first time, that he wanted out. These two boxes were that sentence coming due.

title: Sunday Evening
description:
Sunday evening. {name} taps his father's number.

Two rings, then his father picks up. "Yeah."

"Have you eaten, Dad?"
"Yeah. You?"

Short words back and forth. Seoul weather, Changwon weather. His factory shift is the same as usual. Dad asks if the room is cold; {name} says it is fine.

The words stop, but the call remains connected. On the other end, Dad seems to be waiting for whatever comes next.

description_memory_if_known.relationship_memory:father:father_wellbe: The first time, {name} barely managed to ask, “What about you, Dad?” Today, the exchange lasts a few words longer.
description_memory_if_known.relationship_memory:father:father_future: {name} has already said he thinks things will work out. That promise weighs more heavily in the pauses between today's ordinary words.
description_memory_if_known.relationship_memory:father:father_call_e: Their last call lasted twenty-three seconds. Today, {name} stays through the silence before hanging up.

choices.text: "When I get to Gangnam, you'll be the first one I call." — almost says it, then stops
choices.result_text: Without ever saying the words, {name} presses the end-call button.

choices.text: End the call without saying anything special
choices.result_text:
"Get some sleep, Dad."

After his father answers, "Yeah," {name} ends the call first.

choices.text: "Dad, how have you been?" — asks more
choices.result_text:
"Oh, same as usual," his father says. "You?"

{name} laughs and says, "Same here." His father gives a brief laugh on the other end.

title: A Call Before the Blank
description:
At 8:12 on Sunday evening, {name} reopened the comparison sheet he had completed that week before dialing Father. It placed the names, addresses, and guarantee clauses from Father's repayment papers and the current contract in the same order. Confirmed text was black. Only the route by which Father's document had first arrived remained blank.

Father answered on the third ring. “Yeah. Have you eaten?” After one exchange about the weather in Seoul and Changwon, he asked, “That why you called?”

Three sentences sat side by side in {name}'s notes: ‘Who brought it first?’ ‘I put off visiting all weekend.’ ‘Next Sunday, eight.’ He had already compared the papers and chosen this call to ask about the source. What remained was which sentence would carry the question into the open.

choices.text: Ask the source first: “Who brought this guarantee paper to you?”
choices.result_text:
“This guarantee paper. Who brought it to you first?”

Father did not answer for a while. “Someone I was introduced to brought it. Can't remember the name now.” Then, more quietly, “Why are you looking for that?”

{name} wrote ‘person who was introduced—name unverified’ in the blank. The source narrowed by one step. He still did not say that he had put off the hospital visit all weekend.

choices.text: Before the question, admit that he put off the hospital visit all weekend
choices.result_text:
“Dad. Last weekend, I said I'd visit, then put it off until the weekend was over.”

One long breath crossed the line. “I see.” Father said only that. He did not ask why {name} had postponed it.

{name} offered no excuse. The call log now held the time during which both men knew what had happened. The comparison sheet remained blank because he never asked where the document had come from.

choices.text: If now is difficult, set next Sunday at eight to ask again
choices.result_text:
“If it's hard to talk now, I'll call next Sunday at eight. Have the document open then.”

After a pause, Father repeated, “Eight.” {name} entered the document's filename beside Father's name in the calendar.

He learned no source tonight. What remained beside the ended-call screen was the exact date and time when he would ask for the answer again.

title: Twelve-Week Check
description:
Three months had passed since the final year began.

{name} printed the order history and spread it across the desk. There were two more red lines than green ones. One square remained before the loss limit written in the notebook.

The first train passed outside. The question was not how the story ended. It was whether to spend that final square today.

choices.text: Raise the loss limit by one square and write the order conditions.
choices.result_text:
When {name} rewrote the number beside the limit, the ballpoint pen scored the paper.

He did not press Order yet. Instead, he wrote two lines: the price to enter and the price at which he had to leave.

choices.text: Leave the original loss limit where it is.
choices.result_text:
{name} traced the red line until it grew dark.

Above it sat the price of a Gangnam listing. Below it sat the cash he had kept. Neither disappeared from the page.

choices.text: Place no order today. Record only the open and close.
choices.result_text:
{name} closed the execution window and wrote down only two prices.

There was no action between them. The blank remained. Tomorrow, it could become either evidence or an excuse.

title: After the Result
description:
About a month after the result, a message arrived from Hyunsu.

"Hyung. Everyone says I can just try again. That's the part that scares me most."

A photo of his desk followed. The worn administrative law book leaned shut against the wall. The space where it had lived was an empty square.

{name} wrote a reply, then erased it. Comfort felt too light. Advice came too soon.

choices.text: "Failing the exam doesn't erase the years you gave it." — reply
choices.result_text:
The read mark appeared. Much later came a reply. "I still don't know what those years are worth."

{name} could not tell whether it helped. But for the first time, Hyunsu was speaking about what came after the result.

choices.text: "What are you going to do next?" — ask realistically
choices.result_text:
"I don't know. For the first time, I really don't know."

{name} did not press further. Their silence remained in the message window, without demanding that either of them turn it into an answer.

choices.text: Send a convenience store coffee voucher instead of words.
choices.result_text:
Thirty minutes later, a notification said the voucher had been used. No thanks. No other message.

It only meant Hyunsu had left his room that day. For now, that was enough.

title: First Time in Gangnam Alone
description:
Came to Gangnam for the first time with no one else.

The first glimpse of Gangnam had been a bus-stop ad on the day he arrived in Seoul.
[A city where your place is waiting.]
Today he had taken the subway alone all the way to that sentence.

Walked into a café. The Americano was 9,000 won. Just ordered it.

Sat by the window and looked outside. Well-dressed people walking fast, not looking at each other.

{name} took a sip of coffee.
This is the goal. Or — is it to become someone who belongs here?

choices.text: "I will be back here." — a silent promise
choices.result_text:
Finished the coffee and left. On the subway home, changed the lock screen to a photo of the Gangnam street.

To see it every day.

choices.text: "I'm not even sure this is what I really want." — being honest
choices.result_text:
The coffee went cold. It wasn't that Gangnam was undesirable —
just the first moment of wondering: is this actually what he wants, or is he just refusing to lose?

choices.text: Keep the 9,000-won receipt. Plan to look at it again later.
choices.result_text:
Came home and put the receipt in the desk drawer. Gangnam café. 9,000 won.

Feels like something was confirmed today — just not sure what exactly.

title: Settlement Day
description:
The profit settlement Jaehyuk had promised is next week.

No word from him yesterday. Or today. It had always been like this for the past month — maybe that wasn't strange.

And yet. Why does he keep checking his phone.

Opened KakaoTalk. Last message was Jaehyuk's "How are you" from three weeks ago.
{name}'s reply, "Fine, you?" had gotten back just an emoji.

The money put in keeps cycling as a number in his head.

choices.text: "Hey Jaehyuk, how's everything?" — reach out first
choices.result_text:
No read receipt appeared. One hour. Three hours.

{name} put the phone face-down and tried doing something else. It didn't really work.

choices.text: Wait until settlement day. The message will come.
choices.result_text:
Held out for a week. Learned this time that waiting also takes energy.

The morning of settlement day, {name} woke up early.

choices.text: Message asking to get at least part of it back.
choices.result_text:
"Why all of a sudden? Don't you trust me?" Jaehyuk's reply came back in five minutes.

That fast reply — somehow made it worse.

title: The 1 Left on the Screen
description:
At 11:38 p.m., {name} opened three screens on his phone. His 7:14 message to Jaehyuk — ‘Can you talk tonight? I need to check something’ — still showed the small unread 1. Above it was Jaehyuk's unopened nineteen-page ‘Terms_Final.pdf.’ A deposit-account copy from the hotel listed the bank, account number, and recipient, but not how it connected to the terms.

Twenty-two minutes remained before midnight. {name} had chosen to send one final question with that deadline now. He still had to decide whether to ask about Jaehyuk's intent, demand the source details, or say he would request an independent review. Whichever he chose would be the final question sent.

choices.text: Ask by midnight only whether Jaehyuk intends to keep explaining the transaction
choices.result_text:
{name} sent, ‘Do you intend to keep explaining this transaction? Answer only that by midnight tonight.’ The sent time read 11:39 p.m.

He showed neither the terms nor the deposit-account copy to anyone else. The question also stayed between the two of them. But the issuer, original link, and recipient's relationship all remained outside this last sentence.

choices.text: Demand the issuer, original link, and recipient's relationship together by midnight
choices.result_text:
{name} sent, ‘Can you provide the issuer of these terms, the original link, and the recipient's relationship exactly as written by midnight?’ For the first time, the document name and account name occupied the same bubble.

All three items and the deadline remained in the 11:40 p.m. sent record. He had not opened the material to a third person, but this sentence left less room for their chat to slide back into casual greetings.

choices.text: Say he will request an independent review, then ask Jaehyuk to identify errors by midnight
choices.result_text:
{name} sent Jaehyuk, ‘I'm going to request an independent review of this material. Which facts are wrong? Identify them precisely by midnight.’

The sent record held both the notice of outside review and the reply deadline. The material still remained between the two of them, but the possibility of keeping the conversation private disappeared with the final question.

title: The Missing Timetable
description:
After that, Hyunsu's messages arrived only at dawn. Instead of sentences came photos of convenience store lights or empty buses.

The exam books vanished from his profile. So did the status message that had counted study hours. What he had quit was visible; what he had begun was not.

Tonight, one short line arrived.

"Hyung, what do people do when the timetable disappears?"

choices.text: Write a reply, then erase it.
choices.result_text:
There was nothing to say. Or perhaps too much. {name} wrote several lines, erased them all, and turned off the screen.

One unanswered message remained in the notification panel until morning.

choices.text: "Where have you been? What are you doing?" — ask
choices.result_text:
Much later came a reply. "I sleep in the day. In the evening I sort receipts at a company run by someone I know. Just trying to look at numbers again."

A calculator emoji ended the sentence. Small as it was, it looked like the first mark on an empty timetable.

choices.text: Send a ramyeon voucher and, "Eat. Then sleep."
choices.result_text:
After three in the morning, Hyunsu replied, "You too, hyung." The same words they had traded in the shared kitchen.

{name} looked at them for a long time. The place had changed, but something between them had not broken.

title: The Number: 3 Billion Won
description:
It was past midnight. When the room light went out, only the spreadsheet remained. The laptop fan turned softly; the cursor blinked in the same total-assets cell.

{name} stopped midway through typing three billion won into the target column. At the beginning, the number had been so large it felt weightless. Now it held every month's housing cost, every return, and every night surrendered to it.

Still, it did not feel real. The longer {name} stared, the more meaning drained away until only commas and zeroes remained. Was the goal getting closer, or was {name} disappearing inside the number?

choices.text: Reopened the plan — go back to the numbers
choices.result_text:
The plan is sound, he wrote. The figures are real. Feelings are noise in the calculation. {name} began filling the empty cells one by one.

Change the rate of return and the arrival date moved. Cut living costs and the line climbed a little. Inside the screen, everything had a cause and an effect.

At two in the morning, his wrist had stiffened by the time he closed the final cell. The plan was more precise. The space for why he had begun had not widened at all.

choices.text: Just lay down to sleep.
choices.result_text:
{name} closed the laptop and lay down. In the dark, he said "three billion won" aloud twice. The words had all the meaning of a stranger's password.

The refrigerator motor stopped, and a car passed somewhere in the distance. Those sounds were real in a way the goal was not.

He closed his eyes. Even if he could not feel the destination, his body would rise at the same time tomorrow. Lately, that was how he kept moving.

choices.text: Went out for some air. Walked all the way to the Han River.
choices.result_text:
{name} put on his sneakers and walked to the Han River. Dawn wind slipped under his shirt; dew had made the bench cold. Across the water, lights stretched and trembled.

If it was going to happen once, do it properly. He enlarged the floor plan of the 2.5-billion listing.

One room could be Father's when he came to Seoul. Another could stay empty. The hand that had counted money finally placed people inside the number.

Three billion won. Beneath the target written once more, the shape of a home appeared for the first time.

title: The Six-Month Threshold
description:
On the way back from Gangnam, along the Han River.

He was nearing six months in Seoul.

In the account: {money}. Still nearly 3 billion won away from the goal.

If five years go by at this rate, the math doesn't add up. It can't.

The river moved beyond the railing. Even at night, Seoul was bright.

The lights he had just seen in Gangnam shook across the water. {name} leaned on the railing and thought.
What will I stop seeing while I try to get inside?

choices.text: "Going anyway." — starts walking again
choices.result_text:
I don't know.

Even without a reason, even without confidence it'll work — just go.

That was all. The feet moved first.

choices.text: "There has to be another way." — looks for a shortcut
choices.result_text:
The conventional path won't work.

There's leverage somewhere. Gambling, investment, business — some play that changes everything in one move.

{name} took out his phone. Began searching for something.

choices.text: Just stands there for a while.
choices.result_text:
About ten minutes passed. Made no conclusion.

Just stood there. Watched Seoul's lights spreading across the river.

That felt okay too.

title: First Payday Night
description:
A KakaoBank notification buzzed.

Your monthly salary from {job} has been deposited.

{name} stared at the number for a long time. Until 3 billion — if he saved this amount without spending a single won, how many years would it take? He opened the calculator. Then closed it.

choices.text: Celebrate today. Even small things deserve to be marked.
choices.result_text: Bought a can of beer at the convenience store. 3,800 won. Shelved that long calculation for the night. For now — it's just a first paycheck.
choices.bridge_summary: For one first-payday night, he set that long calculation aside and bought a 3,800-won beer.

choices.text: Open the investment app now. Can't let this money just sit in the account.
choices.result_text: Stared at a list of stocks for an hour. No idea what to put it in. Maybe this is what Sangchul meant by "read the market first."
choices.bridge_summary: On his first payday night, he opened the investment app before he celebrated.

choices.text: Pull up the compound interest calculator. There has to be a faster path.
choices.result_text: 8% compound interest over 21 years. Still far, but having a calculation is different. That's the gap between knowing and not knowing.
choices.bridge_summary: Even at 8% compounding, it was twenty-one years. At least impossibility now had a measurable distance.

title: Convenience Store After Overtime
description:
11 PM. Leaving the office with heavy footsteps.

The team lead from next section was still at his desk. How many years had that person been doing this.

The convenience store lights are visible. Planning to make instant ramyeon and eat alone. Two of today's three meals have been convenience store food.

choices.text: This routine is my reality right now. Something will change if I keep going.
choices.result_text: Finished the ramyeon and walked home. 20 minutes until the last subway. How many more years will I be walking this path?
choices.bridge_summary: After overtime, he ate ramyeon and walked for the last train. For now, this routine was his reality.

choices.text: If overtime keeps up like this, this job isn't my answer. Find another direction.
choices.result_text: Took out the phone and searched job sites. Even if not changing right now, collecting options is different from not collecting them.
choices.bridge_summary: Waiting for the last train, he saved job listings and began collecting ways out of the same overtime.

choices.text: Overtime builds career. This time isn't wasted.
choices.result_text: Folded the ramyeon lid and organized what was learned today. Numbers usable in salary negotiations. Overtime is also strategy.
choices.bridge_summary: He turned what he learned in overtime into career numbers, saving the hours for his next negotiation.

title: First Loss
description:
When the trading terminal opened, a minus sign stood before the unrealized profit and loss. The figure shifted with every refresh, but the sign did not.

Sangchul had called a first loss tuition. The people who hold on are the ones who win, he said. {name} understood the theory. He knew the loss rate, the company's outlook, and the limit he had set in advance. Yet money that had looked like digits at the moment of purchase now took the shape of rent and meals as it shrank.

{name} pressed a palm to his stomach. The market moved on the screen. His body answered first.

choices.text: Sold. His finger hesitated.
choices.result_text:
His finger stopped once above Sell. Past the confirmation window, the loss became final, and the moving figure hardened into one line of trade history.

A message from Sangchul arrived soon after. "The first stop-loss is the hardest. Good job." {name} did not know whether it deserved praise, yet the sentence was strangely comforting.

Closing the app did not return the money. It did leave his body with a memory of where to stop next time.

choices.text: Closed the app. Sangchul's words came back.
choices.result_text:
{name} forced the app closed and silenced its alerts. Knowing the price kept moving unseen was worse. For three days, he picked up the phone and put it down again.

When he finally reopened the app, the loss had been cut in half. Relief came first. Then the knowledge that relief was not proof of a sound decision.

Holding sounded like doing nothing. In practice, it meant choosing not to sell over and over.

choices.text: Put in another 200,000 won. The average cost fell.
choices.result_text:
{name} added 200,000 won. The average cost fell, and the loss percentage looked smaller. The screen looked healthier; more of his money was now trapped inside it.

He told himself the mathematics had improved. He also knew the Sell button felt farther away than it had after the first purchase.

The average went down. The weight of the decision went up. Every move in the chart now carried the new money with it.

title: The First-Year Ledger
description:
After midnight on New Year's Day, {name} spreads the first year's bank records, calendar, and chat list across the desk in his current room. Reduced to a total, the year fits on one line. But beside the income are predawn hours and deadlines, and beside every open door is either a person who reached out or someone he left waiting.

On a blank notebook page, he writes only two possible headings: “What I finished alone” and “What people opened for me.” He has not drawn a dividing line or copied a single name yet.

The first week of the new calendar is still blank. There is room to write one person he will contact first and one time when he will do it.

A blank remains at the end of the right-hand column. He does not fill it with a guess. He folds the first-year ledger with the space intact.

In the message box, he drafts, “Could we talk for a moment this week?” He does not press send. One calendar space and one unsent sentence now wait for the moment when he actually makes contact.

title: Autumn of Year Two
description:
A wedding invitation from Mingi, a high school classmate.

Apartment photos appeared in the group chat too. 'Finally got my own place!' {name} went to hit like, then stopped. He still opened the calculator first whenever he saw a home price. He tried not to compare, but autumn always seemed to pull it out of him.

choices.result_text: Closed the notification. Something complicated lingered. Knowing he's not wrong doesn't make the feeling easy.

choices.result_text: Deleted the app. The first few days, the habit was still there. After two weeks, the stretches of focus got longer. The world felt simpler.

title: The Crossroads at 36
description:
Three years had passed. One afternoon at thirty-six, {name} waited at a Gangnam crosswalk. People poured between glass buildings and crossed without hesitation each time the light turned green.

Less than two years remained. He could finally glimpse where the road behind him was likely to end, which made the question harder: was this the right path, or did he need to believe it was right because he had spent three years on it?

The signal changed once while {name} stood still. A question avoided does not disappear. It only returns at the next crossroads as heavier luggage.

choices.text: His feet moved first.
choices.result_text:
When the light turned green again, his feet stepped out before his thoughts. It was less a choice than momentum built over three years. His mind did not catch up before he reached the other side.

{name} kept the plan unchanged and went to his next appointment. The force of not stopping had brought him this far.

But momentum never checks the destination. Even after the signal went dark, the speed lingering in his soles quietly reminded him.

choices.text: He would change direction. Not cowardice. Reality.
choices.result_text:
{name} erased part of the plan and wrote in a steadier route. The old sentence remained faint beneath the new ink. He decided not to name it surrender or growth.

Reducing volatility might restore his sleep and lower his odds of arriving. He placed both truths on the same line.

Saving the revised plan brought relief and grief together. His body was learning that changing direction did not mean he had stopped walking.

choices.text: He laid out everything he still had. For now, it was enough.
choices.result_text:
{name} wrote down everything he had: money, skills, standards learned through failure, the people who might still answer his calls. He included what could not be reduced to a number.

He had thought his hands were empty, yet the list ran onto a second page. It was not a strong hand, but enough to stay at the table.

He folded the list into his wallet. "Enough" did not promise victory. It meant he could still make the next choice.

title: The Morning After
description:
The morning after the reckoning, the calculator and notebook remained open on the desk.

The figures were unchanged. What {name} had been pretending not to know was not.

Before starting the day, he opened a blank page. Instead of writing what else he could gain, he began with what he was still willing to put at stake.

{name} felt relief and regret at once. He saved the file without erasing either.

title: Six Months
description:
Twenty-four weeks remained. {name} moved between a nighttime photo of Gangnam, the total assets on his phone, and the price of an apartment listing. He knew the exact shortfall now. It looked smaller than it had when unknown, and far more cruel.

For five years, every choice had led into another month. Now there were few months left to recover from one loss, few seasons in which to call the people he had postponed. How he spent the end would remain as clearly as the result.

When the screen went dark, his face overlapped the light in the room. Numbers might decide the ending. They did not have to decide the shape of the final twenty-four weeks.

choices.result_text:
{name} raised the order to the limit. His hand shook over Confirm, then pressed it. The execution chime was brief, far too light a sound for a choice carrying five years.

He refreshed the screen until he finally put the phone down. Everything he could do was finished. Now he could only wait while the market moved.

The tremor in his fingers did not stop. There was no need to decide whether it was fear or hope. There was no way to undo it.

choices.result_text:
{name} calculated everything again from the beginning, separating what he could still reach from what he could not afford to lose. A life did not end without 3 billion won. He stared at that sentence until it no longer sounded like an excuse for defeat.

He erased the reckless cells and kept a plan he could honor. The goal remained, but he would not let it speak for his entire life.

When he saved the file, the screen stamped a time onto the final plan. This, too, was an ending.

{name} shut down the phone and opened the window. Seoul's night wind displaced the heated air in the room. Headlights flowed in the distance; someone passed laughing in the alley below.

The view was wider than the wall beyond his tiny goshiwon window five years ago. He did not yet know whether he had reached Gangnam, but he was no longer standing at the same height.

For a while he calculated nothing. The first moment of the final six months began outside the numbers.

He darkened the screen and saw his face in the glass. At the very end, it became clear that waiting had been a choice too.

title: Two and a Half Years

title: The Cost of Three Lines
description:
On Sunday night, {name} left one light on in his current room and arranged the last three months of records on the floor in date order. One promise had a completion time. Two bore the dates of windows that would not reopen. The record of his body showed care, a deadline, or enduring alone. The family table showed together, alone, or missed.

He checked the times against his phone calendar, payment history, and short notes. A list of completions made the season look fast. A list of closed dates made it look as though he had protected nothing. Each was only half the truth.

{name} held a ruler to a sheet of paper and drew three lines: promise, body, family. He put a slash through any field he could not verify instead of inventing a reason. A damaged record did not give him permission to restore a person or action that was no longer there.

Finally, he set the three records a handspan apart and read them again from the beginning. What belonged on next month's first page was not a resolution. It was the time he had actually arrived, and the date he never did.

He wrote no total beneath the three lines. Combining time spent on a person, time borrowed from his body, and time closed off for money into one score would erase the difference that mattered most.

{name} folded the paper lengthwise and slipped it into the notebook's first page. One white corner remained outside to mark where it should open again. After he cleared the records from the floor, that corner was still visible.

Next month's pace would not begin with a fresh resolution. It would begin by refusing to hide the cost already paid.

title: One and a Half Years
description:
Eighteen months into living in Seoul, {name} reaches for a canned coffee in a convenience-store refrigerator, then rubs his wrist. His body chooses the fastest transfer stairs, the awnings that keep off rain, and the restaurants that stay lit late before he has to think. Whether his room has changed or not, Seoul has entered his habits before it has become an address.

The next month's default schedule is waiting to be copied on his phone. Leaving it alone preserves the pace. Changing one block alters projected income or review time. Closing it for tonight leaves one unfinished line where it is.

Holding the cold can, {name} has to make one of the three actions real.

title: Thirty-Five
description:
Thirty-five.

Started at thirty-three. That means two years have passed.

In Korea, thirty-five carries weight — an age by which things are supposed to have settled. Employment, marriage, a home. A thirty-five-year-old without those three things gets a certain label.

A text from dad: "Happy birthday. You eating okay?"

{name} held the phone for a moment.

choices.result_text: Thirty-five is just a number. Three years to thirty-eight. The plan exists. {name} rewrote tomorrow's task list.

choices.result_text: Closed the planner. Needed one day as {name}, not as the person chasing 3 billion. For once, that felt allowed.

choices.result_text:
"Getting along okay?" Dad asked. Said yes. It wasn't a lie.

title: The Voice Before Midnight
description:
At 11:47 on his birthday night, the call {name} placed connected on the third ring. “What. Birthday's almost over.” A caught breath followed Father's first words. ‘Happy birthday’ on a screen and the voice reaching him now were not the same sentence.

“Have you eaten?”
“I did. You?”

The clock above the call left thirteen minutes before midnight. A photograph of the repayment confirmation remained open on the desk, with a question mark beside the issuing office. {name} could ask first about Father's voice tonight, bring out the remaining document question now, or close the file and give the last minutes of thirty-five only to the call. The call had already begun. What remained was what he would listen for first.

choices.text: “What's wrong with your voice?” Ask about Father tonight first
choices.result_text:
“What's wrong with your voice? You're not sick, are you?”

“I'm not sick. Just haven't talked much today.” Father took a drink of water. When he answered again, his voice had loosened from the first words.

{name} left the document open and listened through Father's breaths and short replies. The call ended at six minutes and twenty-one seconds. The question mark beside the issuing office remained.

choices.text: Ask one sentence now about who issued the repayment confirmation
choices.result_text:
“Dad, after the last payment, where did you get this repayment confirmation?”

“The court issued it.” Father paused. “You called on your birthday to ask about that paper?”

{name} replaced the question mark beside ISSUING OFFICE with COURT. One confirmed field remained, but neither man found his way back to the birthday before the call ended at 11:54.

choices.text: Close the document and say, “Don't hang up until midnight”
choices.result_text:
{name} closed the repayment confirmation. “I won't ask about that tonight. Just don't hang up until midnight.”

Father asked about dinner again without asking why. When the answer ended, neither man made another sentence. As the clock changed to 12:00, Father said, “It's midnight. Get some sleep now.”

The call log read twelve minutes and forty-one seconds. The document's question mark remained, and the final minutes of thirty-five passed with Father still on the line.

title: Saturday Morning
description:
On Saturday morning, the second coffee went cold because {name} had no reason to leave the café. The chair opposite was empty. At the next table, three people laughed while settling on dates for a trip.

He had lived in Seoul for more than two years. At some point, having no one to spend a weekend with had ceased to be either a problem or an event. His contacts were not empty. It was more that he had slowly stopped using the part of himself that reached first.

{name} opened his phone, then set it down. Outside, everyone seemed to be walking toward an appointment. His face wavered faintly on the cold coffee.

choices.result_text:
Scrolling through his contacts, {name} pressed a name he had not called in a long time. The other person answered after three rings. They spoke about weather, work, and getting together sometime.

The call was short. No date was set. Still, the café sounded different after it ended.

{name} finished the cold coffee. One ordinary voice could not fill the empty chair, but it reminded him that he had not fallen out of the world.

choices.result_text:
{name} left the café without a destination. Four hours had passed by the time alleys and avenues opened onto the Han River. His soles burned; river wind cooled the sweat on his back.

From a bench he watched bicycles, strollers, and solitary runners. People who had come together and people who had come alone all faced the same direction beside the water.

The loneliness had not vanished when he turned home. Seoul was simply wide enough that even walking alone did not reach its end.

{name} called no one. He finished the coffee, went home, and started the washing machine. He ate a late lunch while clothes turned behind the glass.

He stretched out on the sofa. He could not remember when being alone had become this familiar. Familiarity was not an answer either.

Good or bad — hard to say. This is just {name} now.

description:
Three years have passed.

title: The Body Speaks
description:
His breathing had not settled even after the subway doors closed. Two stops had passed since the transfer stairs, and the palm gripping the strap was still wet. That had never happened before.

{name} let go of the strap and pressed a thumb to the inside of his wrist. He tried to count ten beats, but lost the number each time the train rounded a curve. His throat was dry, and the cold sweat beneath his shirt would not cool.

A seated passenger stood, leaving an empty place. Trying to look fine, {name} remained on his feet for another stop. He sat only before the next announcement, his bag rising and falling on his knees with every breath.

Looking back, meals had been rushed at convenience stores. Sleep often came after 2 a.m. Exercise had stopped years ago. He could not tell whether this was what thirty-six did, or what came from spending three years borrowing against his time.

Station names slipped past behind his reflection in the dark window. His phone still showed what he had finished today and what was due tomorrow. There was no line for the breath he had just lost.

The doors opened at the next station. Unsure whether to step out, {name} planted both feet against the floor. His body had finished speaking. Only his answer remained.

choices.result_text:
{name} got off at the next station and sat on a platform bench. Once his breathing returned to its usual pace, he opened the appointment screen and chose the earliest slot. One deadline overlapped. This time, he did not close the booking.

A few days later, he described the transfer stairs, two stops, and cold sweat in that order. The doctor looked at his face before the monitor and asked about sleep and meals. The basic tests showed nothing acute.

"Nothing acute does not mean you can keep living this way. Get some exercise, and start by fixing a bedtime."

When he folded the payment receipt into his wallet, the time cleared for the appointment felt more expensive than the bill. Still, for the first time, his body's warning existed as a record instead of a guess.

choices.text: Decided to start eating properly, at least.
choices.result_text:
{name} got off one stop before home and opened the door of the baekban place whose light he always passed. It was near closing. Half the side-dish trays were empty, and the owner reheated the soup before bringing it out.

Only after the first spoonful did he realize that coffee and water were all he had drunk that day. As the warmth moved from his throat to his chest, the dry breath from the train began to loosen. His eyes stung over something this small.

He did not dress one meal up as a cure. On his phone, he saved only the restaurant's closing time and one evening next week when he could actually return. Tonight could not repair the last three years.

But when he paid with an empty bowl in front of him, one fact remained: he had answered his body with today, not later.

At the station convenience store, he bought another strong coffee. The first sip was bitter. By the second, it had no taste. The hand around the cup trembled slightly, but enlarging the figures on his screen made it disappear.

title: 3 AM
description:
3 a.m. Sleep would not come. Without turning on the light in his current room, {name} let the calculator screen glow by itself. He entered the distance to his goal, erased it, and left three billion won as the only sharp object in the room.

There had been a clear reason at first: Father's guarantee fraud, the day he knelt, and the six years spent repaying the debt. On the morning it was finally gone and nothing of his own remained, {name} had decided to build a life no longer shaped by someone else's debt. Three billion won was the form that sentence took.

He entered his current balance and the time remaining again. The answer was correct, but the longer he looked, the less clear it became what the calculation was proving. There was a distance between reaching Gangnam and believing that he had to reach it. No figure marked it.

The last taxi passed outside. The small sounds of the room returned. In daylight, the next task and next deadline pushed the question aside. Here, with no one to answer, it stayed until the end.

Did Gangnam have to happen? Spoken aloud, the question sounded like surrender. Read silently, it sounded like the first time he had placed his own goal back in his own hands.

He could not tell fatigue from maturity or fear. But before closing the calculator tonight, he had to choose which sentence would remain.

{name} pulled the notebook from beneath the calculator and opened its first page. The sentence written after the final repayment was more crooked than the figures, and the corners of the paper had worn smooth under years of handling.

Father. Six years. A guarantee that put someone else's debt under Father's own name. Reading the three again did not tell him whether he felt anger or resolve. So instead of naming the feeling, he wrote down one calculation to verify tomorrow and one block of time to clear for his body.

Restoring the goal to its old place did not erase the costs already paid. Beneath three billion won, {name} wrote, "Do not forget why this began," then drew a line to make sure that sentence could not excuse the people he had missed.

When he switched off the calculator, the room went dark. Certainty had not returned. But he knew what he would carry when he stood again.

He left the notebook open beside the calculator. If the question vanished when he saw the same figures in daylight, it had been exhaustion. If it remained, it belonged to the day as well. His 3 a.m. self would decide neither in advance.

The fact that he had deferred the answer remained on the paper. {name} did not call that a solution. Then he slept.

The calculator left warmth in his palm. Tonight's answer would set the temperature of the final year.

{name} set down the cold cup. Whether that memory was fuel or an excuse could be known only at the end. Today, at least, he could look away from the screen and read the reasons again.

title: Whatever the End
description:
Walking down Gangnam-daero.

Those apartment buildings, actually visible now. Seen this view five years ago too.

Three months left. Whether or not it reaches three billion — the end of this road is in sight. Strangely, it isn't frightening.

Whatever the outcome — these five years are mine.

choices.text: Going to the end. No regrets.
choices.result_text: The steps felt lighter. So much lighter than the first time walking this street, five years ago. Something had changed. It wasn't only the assets.

choices.text: Understood that this is already a drama.
choices.result_text: Not the result — the process is the drama. From 500,000 won at thirty-three, to here. It was already a story. {name} smiled for the first time walking this street.

choices.text: Thought of what he wanted to tell Father when this road ended.
choices.result_text: Not yet. He would say it when this road ended, whether the words reached a phone or a photograph. He still did not know what to say, but he would not postpone it forever.
