title: The Routine Trap
description:
On Monday night, {name} overlays the next four weeks on one calendar. The blocks that produce income are already set to repeat. Travel, meals, and sleep have been pushed into the white space between them. One promised call has been marked “later” three times in a row.

The alarm is set for 6:40 a.m. The last block ends at 11:10 p.m. Copying the schedule unchanged will let it take his body and other people's time first for another month.

Only two actions remain beneath Copy: keep the grid and protect one block first, or actually delete one repeating income block.
description_orthodox:
On Monday night, {name} opens the next four weeks. Eleven minutes to the first trip, one lap of the stairs after lunch, income at the same hours. The checks are precise, but meals and sleep fit only where something else leaves room. A promised call has been marked “later” three times in a row.

The alarm is set for 6:40 a.m. The last block ends at 11:10 p.m. The precise grid is taking his body and other people's time first.

Before copying another month, he must protect one block or actually delete one repeating income block.
description_unorthodox:
On Monday night, {name} overlays four weeks of mismatched colors. The places and jobs change, but every open square attracts another income block. Meals and sleep move last. A chat he meant to answer holds the same “Running late today” three times in a row.

A routine has formed without fixed work. The earliest alarm and latest block take his body and other people's time first.

To copy another month, he must protect one block or actually delete one repeating income block.

choices.text: Keep the repeating grid, but lock one block for a person and my body first
choices.result_text:
{name} marks one Thursday-night block as “Cannot move.” He declines the extra appointment layered over it, then sends a call time to one chat he has left waiting after a meal.

The rest of the repeating grid remains. A gray square appears in the projected-income table. For the first time, the calendar marks time protected first rather than time left over.

choices.text: Delete the latest repeating income block starting next week
choices.result_text:
{name} selects the latest repeating block and presses “Delete from next week.” The confirmation appears twice. He deletes it twice.

The projected-income total drops by one line. In the space it leaves, he writes sleep and the call he still has not returned. The empty outline of the deleted block remains on next week's calendar.

description_if_known.set_morning_routine:
On Monday night, {name} opens the next four weeks beside last year's notebook. Small lines crowd the space beside “7 AM tomorrow,” one for every day he kept it. Meals and sleep have still been pushed into leftover squares, and a promised call has been marked “later” three times.

The alarm remains set for 6:40 a.m. The last repeating block ends at 11:10 p.m. A calendar full of proof that he kept going is taking his body and other people's time first.

Before copying another month, he must protect one block or actually delete one repeating income block.

title: Mom and Dad Come to Seoul
description:
On the Saturday his parents come to Seoul, their train arrives at Seoul Station at five. Their return ticket to Changwon is for 9:10 that night.

“We're coming to Seoul Saturday. Your mother too.”
“What for?”
“Do I need a reason to see your face?”

At Seoul Station, Father checks the return ticket before anything else. Mother hands {name} a bag of side dishes. “After dinner, let us see where you live for a minute.”

It is past six when the food arrives near the station. To visit the room and make the train, they have to pay and leave now. Staying at the table gives the three of them a longer dinner, but his parents will once again leave without seeing the door where he lives. Father puts down his chopsticks. “You decide. The train won't wait.”
description_low_mental:
On the Saturday his parents come to Seoul, their train arrives at five and their return ticket to Changwon is for 9:10 that night. {name} pushes the laundry in his room to one side. There is nowhere to put the face of a man who has not slept.

At the station, Father asks instead of greeting him, “Are you sleeping?” “I am.” Father studies his face longer than the answer. Mother hands him a bag of side dishes heavy enough for both hands.

At the restaurant, Mother says she wants to see his room. To visit it and make the train, they have to pay and leave now. If they stay at the table, his parents will once again return to Changwon knowing only the station and restaurant. Father lays the return ticket on the table. “You decide whether we eat longer or see where you live.”

choices.text: Stay at the table, finish dinner, and do not show them the room
choices.result_text:
{name} orders another stew and turns his phone facedown. Mother places meat on his plate. Father starts the story of the Changwon factory again from the beginning.

At the gate, Father pushes the side-dish bag toward {name}. “We'll see the address next time.” While his parents tap their tickets, he never says where the room is.

After the train leaves, sesame oil slips through the closed lids when he lifts the bag. Dinner lasted longer. The Seoul his parents know still ends at the station and restaurant.

choices.text: Cut dinner short and take them to his current room
choices.result_text:
{name} packs the remaining food and heads to his current room with his parents. Mother keeps the side-dish bag on her knees during the ride. Father checks the return-train time twice.

When the door opens, Mother asks where to put the side dishes. Father removes his shoes and looks slowly around the room. “So this is where you live.” He adds neither judgment nor comfort.

The three drink a brief cup of tea from paper cups on the desk. The words they did not finish over dinner remain. His parents save the room's address in their message for the trip home.

title: The End of the Second Year
description:
His second year in Seoul was drawing to a close.

At the door, he felt for the key in his pocket. The room might have changed since the beginning, or it might not have. His body now knew the subway lines, the cheaper convenience stores, and the gukbap places that stayed open late.

Another season had passed since the night he counted a year and a half. Was he a Seoulite now?

Not quite. Seoul was still strange, and home was no longer familiar in the old way. Somewhere between them was where he lived.
description_orthodox:
The second year in Seoul was drawing to a close.

The record was real: consistent work, money accumulating. But the gap between where he stood and where he needed to be was still enormous.

{name} recalculated, quietly, without telling anyone.
description_unorthodox:
The second year in Seoul was drawing to a close.

He had taken angles others would not. Some paid off. Some did not.

The city was becoming familiar, not conquered.

{name} could not tell whether that was progress or adaptation.

choices.text: Closed his hand around the key. His body had memorized Seoul first.
choices.result_text:
Transfer corridors, late-night restaurants, and the awnings that kept off rain came to him before he had to think.

He could not call himself a Seoulite. His body had still learned how to move through a day in this city.

choices.text: Urgency could become fuel.
choices.result_text:
Some days, urgency became energy.

{name} hoped this would be one of them.

title: A Saturday Never Sent
description:
On the third Saturday of September, the new room held neither the sound of a washing machine nor a television. Three unsent lines remained in Notes on {name}'s phone: "Want to meet after your shift?" "I never answered you then." "The room I moved into is all right." He had moved none of them into an actual conversation.

He had contacted no one first this month. There was no sent time and nowhere to arrive. Saturday's calendar square was blank. At 8:47 p.m., only a delivery-app discount appeared at the top of the screen. A motorcycle passed down the alley, its sound slipping through the window frame. {name} lowered the screen brightness, opened the Notes list again, and looked between it and the empty calendar.

choices.text: Delete all three messages
choices.result_text:
{name} opened each note and erased the words from the end. When the last "all right" disappeared, only a cursor remained on the empty page.

After the screen went dark, his thumb pressed the blank space at the bottom once more. It made no sound.

choices.text: Leave the messages as drafts, unsent
choices.result_text:
{name} closed Notes without sending a word. No notification count changed. Only three saved drafts remained in the list.

On the calendar, he wrote only "Contact." The spaces for a name and time beneath it remained blank.

choices.text: Leave the phone and go to the laundromat
choices.result_text:
{name} carried a bag of laundry to the end of the alley. Behind round windows, strangers' shirts and towels turned together. The plastic chair across from him was empty.

Saturday was nearly over when the dryer stopped. The folded clothes were warm. Back in the room, there were no new messages on the phone.

title: The First Utility Bill
description:
At 7:12 p.m., one month after the move, confirmation arrived that the first electric bill had been paid. {name} unfolded the notice that had been wedged beneath the door and set it beside the transfer receipt. It was the first price attached to a full month in this room.

On the calendar where {name} had redrawn his commute and mealtimes, only the first three days bore check marks. The last box and unfamiliar ceiling from move-in night were already behind him. The room now smelled of dry towels and carried the marks of a month's living. The light above the sink blinked once, and the refrigerator motor started again. {name} wrote the payment time in the calendar margin.

choices.text: Tape the transfer receipt above the desk
choices.result_text:
{name} wrote the amount beneath the rent date and taped the receipt to the wall. When one corner lifted, he pressed it down with his thumbnail for a long time.

He copied the same amount into next month's square. This was no longer the new room. It was his current address, with a price due every month.

choices.text: Send Father one line saying the room works fine
choices.result_text:
{name} took a photo that showed both the boiler light and the bill. He wrote, "The electricity works. The room isn't cold."

After a while, Father replied, "Good." That one word remained beneath the room photo. {name} put the phone face down on the bill.

choices.text: Rewrite the abandoned routine from the current time onward
choices.result_text:
{name} did not fill the missed squares with late check marks. Starting with the next blank, he wrote tonight's dinner, tomorrow's alarm, and one period of rest this week.

When he set down the pen, the refrigerator motor stopped. A brief silence belonging only to his room arrived, something he could never have heard in the goshiwon.

title: Writing the Renewal Alone
description:
The new rent on the renewal notice overlaps a fold in the first lease. At 5:34 p.m. on Friday, {name} spreads the two papers side by side on the desk in his current room. The new rent is higher, and the new end date sits one year away. The landlord wants an answer by six.

There is one signature box. With no one else to decide or compare for him, he has to price the cost of keeping this address against the cost of moving again. Accepting a year preserves the room and reduces what he can spend each month. Asking for a shorter term changes the deposit. Refusing means beginning another room search tonight.

{name} touches the new rent and the remaining cash with the tip of his pen. In twenty-six minutes, the thing he has to protect is not a relationship but his address for the next season.

choices.text: Accept the higher rent and sign a one-year renewal
choices.result_text:
{name} rereads the new rent and end date, then signs the one-year renewal. The landlord confirms it at 5:49.

The address stays. In the first line of his notebook, {name} writes the amount he will have to cut each month. Filling one empty signature box fixes the cost of the next twelve months with it.

choices.text: Ask for six months and compare the larger deposit
choices.result_text:
{name} asks for six months instead of a year. The landlord keeps the rent unchanged but answers with a larger deposit.

{name} places the account balance beside the added deposit and signs the shorter term. Freedom to move will return sooner; the cash available now becomes trapped in the room instead.

choices.text: Decline renewal and set the move-out inspection now
choices.result_text:
{name} declines the renewal and sets an inspection date with the landlord. At 6:02, the time by which the room has to be empty enters his calendar.

He avoids the higher rent and fixes the end of this address at the same time. The unsigned renewal and next month's schedule with no new address remain side by side on the desk.

title: The Weekend of the Changwon Hospital Room
description:
On Friday night, a photo from Mother shows the ward and room number at a Changwon hospital. Father is on his third day as an inpatient, with his discharge to be reviewed Monday afternoon. Father has sent nothing.

The KTX screen still offers the first train Saturday and a ticket arriving Monday morning. Going Saturday spends the weekend at the hospital. Going Monday leaves {name}'s own arrival two days later. Sending only money to the hospital account requires no ticket, but it also means not opening the room during this admission.

Mother's last line says, “If you're coming, just tell me the date.” {name} puts his ID into a bag, then takes it out again. The decision now is not whether some other promise counts as complete, but when his body will reach Father's hospital room.

choices.text: Buy the first KTX on Saturday and open the hospital-room door this weekend
choices.result_text:
{name} buys the first KTX seat and sends Mother the arrival time. The open hours on the weekend calendar fill with Changwon travel and hospital visiting time.

When he opens the room on Saturday morning, Father turns from the bed by the window. “You came.” {name} takes the ID and ticket from his pocket and sets them on the bedside cabinet. The time he opened the door during this admission remains with those two objects.

choices.text: Buy a Monday-morning arrival ticket and send Mother the date
choices.result_text:
{name} buys a ticket arriving in Changwon on Monday morning and sends it to Mother. “I'll go straight to the room then,” he writes, adding the exact train number.

Mother's read receipt appears, but no reply follows. The hospital door stays closed through the weekend. The screen holds the Monday ticket, the room number, and an arrival postponed by two days.

choices.text: Send money toward the hospital bill and say he cannot come during this admission
choices.result_text:
{name} transfers money to the hospital account Mother sent and writes, “I can't come during this admission.” He does not turn the reason for the money and the reason for his absence into the same sentence.

Once the transfer receipt is saved, he closes the KTX search. The room number moves higher in Mother's chat. Instead of the hospital door, he holds a receipt bearing the recipient's name and the send time.

title: A Name on Page Eighteen
description:
At 8:42 Monday morning, the original file labeled GD-P25-R3 arrived in the electronic contract box. {name} downloaded all eighteen pages. The first listed a purchase price of 2.58 billion won and a 258 million won deposit. Page eleven set a 320 million won equity-loss cap, followed in small type by costs excluded from that cap.

On the last page, the proposed jointly liable party field already read Kim Daeun. There was no signature. The deposit deadline was Friday at 3 p.m., and the gap against the available balance was 70 million won. {name} reduced the zoom until the three figures and one name fit on the same screen. Only warm glass lay beneath his fingers.

choices.text: Copy the purchase price, deposit, and current gap onto one line
choices.result_text:
{name} wrote down 2.58 billion won, 258 million won, and the 70 million won gap in order. Beneath them, he added that the Friday deposit would remain short unless he touched money reserved for existing obligations.

Once every figure was written, the blank looked sharper than before. His pen stopped beside the shortfall while the time left before the deposit deadline kept shrinking on-screen.

choices.text: Open and read only the exceptions to the loss cap
choices.result_text:
{name} enlarged the fine print beneath the bold 320 million won figure. Dispute costs and early-recovery fees sat outside the cap. The largest number on the page was not the true edge of the loss.

He underlined both exceptions and saved one screenshot. The bold ceiling and the small exceptions glowed at different sizes inside the same image.

choices.text: Keep Daeun's name field and the unsigned line in the same image
choices.result_text:
{name} enlarged the last page and saved the typed name with the empty signature line. Not one character had been written by Daeun. The file properties showed only the R3 revision time and the author account.

He noted, ‘No confirmation from the named party.’ He did not send a removal request yet. The cursor blinked steadily over the white signature line.

title: The Uncut File
description:
At 9:16 Wednesday night, {name} staged the GD-P25-R3 original in his chat with Sangchul: eighteen pages, 6.4 megabytes. He attached no summary and no cropped image hiding the name field. The preview included the purchase price, loss cap, and the final page bearing Daeun's name.

Only one line remained blank beneath the send button. Leading with the 70 million won gap would expose his weakness. Leading with joint liability would expose a name he had not yet discussed with Daeun. Leading with Friday at 3 p.m. would tell Sangchul who was desperate. Once the file could no longer be reduced, {name} chose which fact would become the first sentence.

choices.text: Send the full original with the 70 million won gap in the first line
choices.result_text:
{name} wrote, ‘The current gap is 70 million won. Please start there,’ and sent all eighteen pages. At 9:18, the screen recorded one file sent.

There was no room left to hide his balance. Sangchul had not answered; only the shortfall {name} chose to expose remained at the bottom of the chat.

choices.text: Send the full original and flag the joint-liability language first
choices.result_text:
{name} wrote, ‘Please read the name field on the last page with the liability range on page eleven,’ then sent the original. The transfer record showed that no page had been cut.

There was no indication that Sangchul had read it. The time Daeun's name had remained in the draft passed into the chat along with the revision history.

choices.text: Send the full original and lead with the Friday 3 p.m. deadline
choices.result_text:
{name} wrote, ‘The deposit deadline is Friday at 3 p.m.,’ and transmitted the whole file. The timestamp beside its name read 9:19.

Now the other side knew who was short on time. He added no line demanding an answer. A Friday calendar alert vibrated once above the chat he had left open.

title: The Six O'Clock Answer
description:
At 4:12 the following Monday, the closing manager on an existing acquisition-advisory job demanded an answer. The final fee was 18 million won. Delivering the reconciled material by midnight kept the terms intact. Disclosing the 70 million won gap allowed a request for one more day. A third closing sheet reduced the fee to 12 million won in exchange for providing no additional joint-liability material.

The response window ended at 6 p.m. R3 was already open behind it. At six, the thing that would close was not the contract but this reply field. {name} set the clear folder holding R3 beside the keyboard and moved one of the three sentences into the actual reply field.

choices.text: Disclose the gap and request one more day
choices.result_text:
{name} entered the 70 million won gap and the single day he needed, then sent the extension request. A receipt time of 4:37 appeared, but no approval did.

A chance to buy time had placed his cash position in the other side's hands. The monitor held an unanswered request number on one side and the unchanged shortfall on the other.

choices.text: Keep the current terms and commit to the midnight delivery
choices.result_text:
{name} accepted the current terms and opened the submission window due before midnight. Once travel and a meal were removed from the seven hours left, only six working hours remained.

The 18 million won fee did not shrink. Instead, every open block that evening turned into a file number. The phone lit and went dark several times beneath the clear folder.

choices.text: Refuse the added liability material and close at the lower fee
choices.result_text:
{name} wrote that he would provide no additional joint-liability material and selected the 12 million won closing sheet. The expected fee fell by 6 million won when the response was recorded.

The price of withholding another person's name became a number immediately. Only the reduced fee and the 4:41 submission time remained side by side.

title: Where Her Name Was Removed
description:
At 8:10 Saturday night, {name} opened a clear folder at the last window table in a cafe. The final page of R3 contained ‘Kim Daeun.’ The same field in R4-SELF, revised after the removal request, was blank. Without her name, the financing ceiling had fallen from 1.18 billion won to 760 million won. The 420 million won difference lay at the center of the table.

Daeun looked first at her unsigned name, then at the blank. She set a blue mechanical pencil between the two documents.

“Minjun, am I supposed to thank you for taking it out? Why didn't you tell me when it went in?”

{name} could not answer with the word protection. Only the order in which he exposed the removed name and the lost figure remained.

choices.text: Read the lost 420 million won aloud first
choices.result_text:
{name} read the old ceiling, the new ceiling, and the difference in order. Daeun drew a short line beneath 420 million won.

“Don't say it like that was the price of my name. If it's money you gave up, tell me in your own words why you gave it up.”

{name} could not erase the figure. The blue line remained under it, and the empty name field looked whiter beside it.

choices.text: Show the original draft time beside the removal-request time
choices.result_text:
{name} placed the R3 authoring time beside the time he requested the removal. Daeun traced the time between them with one finger.

“Keeping me safe and deciding without me aren't the same. During that time, I didn't even know where my name was.”

{name} looked up without turning off the screen. The corners of the two versions sat misaligned inside the clear folder.

choices.text: Open the weekend-and-night clause beside the name field
choices.result_text:
{name} unfolded the addendum promising priority access to weekends and nights. Daeun studied that sentence longer than the blank name field.

“My name is gone. But if all your nights are in here, this contract is still spending my time too.”

With the blue pencil, Daeun drew a vertical line between ‘nights’ and ‘priority.’ The paper did not tear; only the sentence split in two.

title: Before a Name Entered the Field
description:
After the shutter came down at Jiyeon's Seoul office, {name} opened the initial contract on the folding table. The JOINTLY LIABLE PARTY field was blank; a review note beside it said only, ‘Han Jiyeon may be included.’ No name or signature had entered the document, yet the field already looked as though it were waiting for a person.

Jiyeon pressed a nail to the note, then covered the blank with a sticky tab.

“Oppa, if my name could go there, I see it first. Minseo reviews it. We can't let Sangchul explain Sangchul's own paper and call that a review.”

“I understand,” {name} said, opening the copy for Minseo. Jiyeon wrote LEE MINSEO in the independent-reviewer box. The question was no longer whether to seek her consent, but which hidden cost of the blank would lead the review.

choices.text: Ask first why the joint-liability field exists
choices.result_text:
Jiyeon boxed the blank and wrote, ‘Why is a person's field needed before the price or scope is fixed?’ {name} sent that page with the reviewer designation to Minseo.

No answer appeared beneath the sent time. But the reason a person's name had been raised for a deal's convenience was now the first question. The liability cap and weekend clause remained unmarked in the same copy.

choices.text: Mark the maximum liability her name could carry
choices.result_text:
{name} aligned the joint-liability field with the liability-cap clause. Jiyeon drew a blue question mark on the blank limit and wrote, ‘If my name enters, where does my part end?’

He sent both pages with the reviewer designation to Minseo. The number came first; why it had to be Jiyeon, and who would take her nights, remained outside the opening question.

choices.text: Send the name field beside the weekend-and-night clause
choices.result_text:
Jiyeon held the pages so the empty name field and PRIORITY ACCESS TO WEEKENDS AND NIGHTS fit in one photograph. “Ask Minseo why these belong in the same contract.”

{name} sent the photograph with the reviewer designation. Only a sent time remained. Shared time had been exposed before the financial ceiling, while the reason the joint-liability field existed moved to the next question.

title: The Empty Chair at Nine
description:
At 8:37 Monday morning, the team lead held open the new-business meeting room and handed {name} an appointment proposal. The role lasted twelve months, added 450,000 won a month, and required repayment of six million won in training costs if he left early. But the team lead pointed not to a clause, but to the empty chair in the nine o'clock meeting.

“You can sign later. Sit there today and move the team.” He slid over a temporary pass. “The company hasn't granted the authority yet. The people in that room will still see a lead.”

Three people waited inside for someone to speak first. The company could reclaim borrowed authority that evening. Before then, it would wear down the team lead's expectation, his coworkers' trust, or {name}'s time. The proposal was only the paper left afterward.

choices.text: Enter the meeting, but tell the team he is not their lead yet
choices.result_text:
{name} sat in the empty chair and placed the temporary pass on the table. “I did receive an appointment proposal. Today's authority is only borrowed.” The last employee to arrive pulled the laptop closer, then turned it back when {name} asked about the week's work.

The team lead listened from the doorway until the meeting ended. Taking back the pass, he said, “Transparency is good. I'll also remember that you deferred the authority before the company entrusted you.” The meeting was finished, but the formal appointment decision moved to Monday. No one said whether the next proposal would carry the same name.

choices.text: Stay with the team lead until he hears why he was chosen
choices.result_text:
{name} pushed the pass aside. “Did you choose me because I'm good, or because no one else will carry this?” The team lead checked the time after the first question. After the second, he sat down. He said he needed someone who would remain after inheriting last quarter's failure.

After hearing him, {name} picked up the pass, entered late, and sat in the empty chair. Another senior employee had already set the first direction. He did not reverse it; he took the remaining reports and the afternoon explanation himself. He used the borrowed authority, but lost the right to set the first course. He knew why he had been chosen. The team now waited to see whether the reason was true.

choices.text: Take today's work under borrowed authority and send the team home on time
choices.result_text:
{name} hung the temporary pass around his neck and sat in the empty chair. He moved the overdue reports to his own queue and gave the three employees only what they could finish before leaving. “I'll stay with the rest.” The team lead did not stop him. The team did not thank him yet.

After ten, one block of office light remained. The first proposal lay folded beneath the monitor; the temporary pass was still on {name}'s neck. He had protected everyone else's evening, but the authority had never become his. The team lead left only a message asking for his answer tomorrow.

title: Twenty Minutes Left in the Evening
description:
At 9:14 Wednesday night, {name} joined his scheduled call with Minseo from his room. The appointment proposal lay on his desk. Minseo kept her coat on; she had cleared twenty minutes before leaving to pick up her child. When {name} raised the paper, she shook her head.

“I'm not the person who gives you that seat or takes it away. The figures can wait.” Minseo glanced toward the clock by her door. “On the day you sat in that chair, whom did you make stay late?”

{name} looked at the first page: twelve months, 450,000 won a month, six million won in training costs. Taking the rest of Minseo's evening might bring more counsel. Ending the call meant no one would decide for him tomorrow. The paper stayed on the desk. What crossed the distance first would be something said to a person.

choices.text: Tell Minseo first that he already used authority the team lead had only lent him
choices.result_text:
{name} told her about the moment he sat in the empty chair, the borrowed pass, and the faces that had waited in the meeting room. Minseo did not interrupt until the end. “Did you tell the team that the authority was only borrowed for today?”

When {name} could not answer at once, Minseo picked up her bag. “Then return those words before you return the document.” A door opened beyond her screen. The call ended on time, and the first proposal was never sent. He had hidden less from Minseo, but what he owed the team had grown heavier by morning.

choices.text: Tell Minseo to go pick up her child and face the team lead alone tomorrow
choices.result_text:
{name} closed the proposal. “Go. I won't use the rest of your evening for my decision.” Minseo watched the screen for a moment, then zipped her coat.

“Don't call protecting my time the right answer. It becomes your life, {name}, only if the same answer holds when I'm not there.” The call ended. Only the refrigerator and the folded first page remained in the room. The cost of giving up her counsel was twenty minutes returned to Minseo. The silence before tomorrow's team lead now belonged entirely to {name}.

choices.text: Ask her to stay twenty minutes more and say why he needs the title so badly
choices.result_text:
{name} spoke all at once: what 450,000 won meant now, and how fear of being unemployed again had put him in the chair first. Then he asked her for twenty more minutes.

Minseo did not check the clock. “If I give you my evening, does that make the role safer, or only make you less afraid?” She waited for {name}'s answer without taking off her coat. “This is as far as I listen tonight.” The door closed, then the call. The proposal remained unsent. Only the cost of the request had reached the space between them.

title: After Hyunsu Gets Off Work
description:
At 4:20 the following Tuesday, the team lead pointed to the blank external-reviewer field on the meeting-room screen. One accounting-firm employee could cut approval from fifteen business days to five. “Give me a name today.” The temporary pass remained beneath his finger.

{name} called Hyunsu. Stepping away before finishing work for a client, Hyunsu heard the request. “Hyung, if my firm's name goes there, I have to explain here why I did it. Don't spend my standing at work as the price of ten days.”

Across the table, the team lead waited. Making Hyunsu deliver the refusal would spare {name} one sentence. Drawing the line himself could cost the borrowed authority first. Waiting until Hyunsu finished work would take today's approval and Hyunsu's evening together.

choices.text: Ask Hyunsu to tell the team lead the refusal himself
choices.result_text:
{name} set the phone in the center of the table and switched on the speaker. Hyunsu told the team lead clearly not to use his name or his employer. The team lead asked nothing more, and the approval schedule returned to fifteen days.

Before hanging up, Hyunsu lowered his voice. “Don't hand me the sentence you have to say, hyung. Even the decision not to use my name has to come from your seat.” A refusal remained in the room, but it belonged to Hyunsu. {name} had spent his relationship and an interruption in Hyunsu's work to avoid one sentence before the team lead.

choices.text: End the call and say himself that he will wait ten days without Hyunsu's name
choices.result_text:
{name} told Hyunsu, “I won't use your name or your firm,” and ended the call first. Then he faced the team lead. “I will explain to the team why we are late instead of buying speed with him.”

The team lead picked up the temporary pass. “Then this authority waits until the appointment is formal.” The light cord slid from {name}'s neck. He spent no more of Hyunsu's day, and approval returned to fifteen days. In exchange, tomorrow's empty chair and every decision he could no longer make came back to him.

choices.text: Send the team lead away and apologize to Hyunsu after he gets off work
choices.result_text:
{name} said, “I won't press someone for an answer while he's working.” The team lead confirmed that today's approval and temporary authority would both expire, then left the room.

After eight, Hyunsu came as far as the office entrance. {name} did not take out the paper. “I'm sorry I pulled you away from work and tried to hand you the refusal I owed.” Hyunsu remained standing. “What I refuse is mine. What you tell your company is yours. Next time, tell me what you will lose before you say my name.” The field stayed empty. Approval, authority, and an hour from both men were gone. What remained was Hyunsu's boundary, heard from its beginning.

title: A Ring Beyond the Offer
description: On Friday evening, failure alerts spread down one side of the startup office monitors. The co-founder said the acquirer valued the company at KRW 16 billion and had offered KRW 3.2 billion for {name}'s twenty-percent stake. They had not imagined that number on the day {name} put in KRW 3 million and said he would start with the co-founder. As the team looked toward the offer between them, {name}'s phone rang again. The screen showed Sujin, a current customer who had been reporting the same failure. The acquirer was waiting for an answer, and the team was waiting to see whom the founders would face first. “You're taking it, right?” the co-founder asked. The offer stayed on paper while Sujin's time was already being lost.

choices.text: Turn the offer face-down and answer Sujin with the co-founder and team listening
choices.result_text:
{name} turned the offer face-down so KRW 3.2 billion disappeared and switched on the speaker. “Sujin, I'm listening.” She described when the login had dropped and which screen had failed again. The team returned to their monitors, and the co-founder told the acquirer to wait.

They still had not found the cause, and Sujin did not say the service was fine. Everyone listened for her next words until another missed call from the acquirer appeared. The time Minseo had agreed to meet at the cafe was drawing just as close.

title: The Untouched Second Cup
description: The cafe had announced closing time before {name} arrived. Sujin's service was working for now, though the same failure could return, and one of the two drinks Minseo had ordered was already cold. As {name} began to mention KRW 3.2 billion, a voice message from the co-founder arrived. “The customer is stable for now. The team is still waiting. Don't come back with only the price.” Minseo listened without telling him to sell or stay. “KRW 3.2 billion may be the goal you've chased. But who is giving up tonight to get you there? That's the life the number leaves out.” She returned the decision to {name}. “If I choose it for you, you'll bring me back tomorrow.” A worker began stacking chairs for the second time.

choices.text: Leave the untouched second cup and return to the office
choices.result_text:
{name} stood without touching the drink Minseo had saved for him. She did not ask about the place they had meant to visit or the meal they had meant to share. She only said, “Next time, don't come for an answer. Come tell me what you answered.”

When the door closed, their promised evening remained beside the cold cup. No more messages came from the co-founder on the way back. Only the office light where the team waited stayed on at the end of the alley.

title: The People Left at the Door
description: Late at the office, the team learned that the acquirer's name had circulated in the meeting room before anyone spoke to them. People stopped at the door with their coats on. Looking toward the window, the co-founder told {name}, “Don't cast me as the one you protected, then make me face the team for you.” The acquirer wanted both founders on a call shortly and would not hold the time for long. Calling the team back could cost that meeting and the remaining secrecy. If {name} stayed while the co-founder took the call alone, he would lose control of his own terms and leave one person carrying both voices. If both founders went, the team would go home unanswered. Whom they faced first had become the cost they were choosing.

choices.text: Call the team back and explain everything together from the beginning
choices.result_text:
Instead of stopping people at the door, {name} set the meeting-room chairs back out. The co-founder sat beside him, not across from him. They took turns explaining that an acquisition offer had arrived and that neither had decided what to do.

Questions continued past the acquirer's call slot, and the request for secrecy could no longer mean the same thing. The team's faces did not soften. Still, no one had hidden behind the other while speaking tonight.

choices.text: Stay with the team and send the co-founder alone to the acquirer call
choices.result_text:
{name} asked the team to sit while the co-founder took the call. He heard fragments of the co-founder's voice through the closed meeting-room door, but not which conditions the acquirer was changing. {name} answered the team's questions only as far as he knew.

They were not left alone, but {name} missed the first discussion of his own stake and future role. The co-founder carried both founders' voices alone. After the call, one expression could not show everything it had cost.

choices.text: Go to the acquirer together and send the team home unanswered
choices.result_text:
{name} said he could not answer tonight and left with the co-founder. The people at the door folded their questions and scattered toward the elevator. With the acquirer, both founders heard the price and future roles in the same room.

When they returned, the office was dark and no one had spoken first in the team chat. “Tomorrow, you go first,” the co-founder said. They kept the fast meeting, but the years in which the team trusted the founders to speak first had not remained untouched.

title: Fifty Million
description:
{name} turned the calculator off, then on again. The figure remained: 50,000,000 won. Its eight digits looked too bright in the room.

Three billion won was still far away; every calculation made the remaining distance more exact. Yet he had begun with 500,000 won, a balance that once made rent frightening. It had grown a hundredfold, carrying luck, endurance, and several choices he could never make the same way again.

He covered the number with one finger, then revealed it. For the first time, possibility looked less like a feeling than evidence. The refrigerator sounded exactly as it had yesterday.

choices.text: Tell no one. Walk to the convenience store and buy something expensive.
choices.result_text:
Telling anyone would mean explaining only the number. {name} pocketed his phone and went down to the convenience store. He chose the 5,000-won ice cream he usually passed over.

On the goshiwon stairs, cold mist clung to his fingers as he opened it. The first bite was too sweet. From the second, it tasted like ordinary ice cream.

He liked that no one knew what he was celebrating. Long after it was gone, the wooden stick remained in his hand.

choices.text: Dial Father's number — knowing it will not connect.
choices.result_text:
{name} tapped the name saved as Father. He even prepared a sentence for the amount. After a short signal, however, a recording said the number could not be reached.

He knew the recording and did not need to hear it through. When he ended the call, the outgoing log held one new timestamp. This was not an unanswered call. There was no one left who could answer.

The figure on the calculator had not changed. Only the person he had wanted to show had come into sharper focus.

choices.text: Set the next target immediately — 500 million.
choices.result_text:
On paper, {name} wrote 500,000 won, 50 million won, then 500 million won. The next box held 3 billion won. Arrows between them made a staircase.

Instead of marking 50 million as a victory, he underlined it and began calculating the next step. The pleasure had nowhere to linger.

An impossible wall had divided into several ledges. At the same time, he could finally see the full height left to climb.

title: A Number That Can't Be Shared
description:
The total-assets figure crossed 100 million won. The banking app displayed it without ceremony. {name} refreshed twice, then opened his contacts.

He wanted to tell someone. Father's name remained where it had been, but the number no longer connected. With a friend, he would probably lower the amount before saying it, afraid it might sound like boasting. Yet he could not immediately think how many friends were still close enough to worry about.

His thumb drifted over the names. He pressed none of them and turned off the screen. In the black glass, the number vanished and left only his face.

choices.text: Open Father's contact — try to remember his last voice.
choices.result_text:
{name} opened Father's contact, then the call records that remained. The screen held dates, times, and call lengths, but no voice. From the screen alone, he could not even tell which few words had been the last.

{name} reached for the short breaths and one or two phrases he could remember. He added no sentence he was unsure of. The voice stopped where the memory did.

The 100 million won remained a number he had told no one. He placed the contact and the balance on the same screen for a moment, then closed both.

choices.text: Told no one — decided to keep it to himself.
choices.result_text:
The number was his. It needed neither explanation nor witness. {name} closed his contacts and reopened the spreadsheet.

He marked the 100-million-won cell and entered the next target. The cursor moved right without hesitation. He had begun alone; celebrating alone should be natural too.

As the night deepened, that sentence grew smoother. No one's name remained in it.

choices.text: Bought a can of beer alone at the convenience store — a private toast.
choices.result_text:
{name} sat in a plastic chair outside the convenience store and opened a can of beer. Foam flecked the back of his hand. He raised the can slightly toward the balance glowing on his phone.

People passed with umbrellas and grocery bags. None of them knew someone here had crossed 100 million won today. The beer was warmer than he expected.

When the can was empty, he turned off the screen. The celebration was over, but the crush of aluminum sounded unusually loud.

title: Gangnam Property Prices
description:
Opened the real estate app.

Gangnam-gu apartments. The cheapest one at 1.7 billion. Then 2 billion, 2.5 billion, 3.5 billion.

The day his assets passed 2 billion, he had only looked up at lit windows from the street. Now the number was 2.5 billion. The cheapest listing was technically within reach. Was entering Gangnam just a matter of tapping one of those prices?

Acquisition tax, brokerage fees, and monthly maintenance sat below the photographs in smaller type. Having 2.5 billion in assets was not the same as being able to spend 2.5 billion on a home.

He had never properly considered the difference.

choices.text: Bookmarked the 1.7 billion one — this is the target.
choices.result_text:
Pinned it on the map. Eight minutes from Line 2. South-facing. 109 square meters.

No one stood in the photographed living room. For the first time, he calculated what could go inside it after liquidating assets and paying the taxes.

One listing remained in his saved folder. Vague Gangnam had become an address.

choices.text: Closed the app — not reality yet.
choices.result_text:
Looking too closely made it frightening. Reach 3 billion first. Think afterward. He closed the app.

His face appeared in the black screen. He had spent almost five years chasing the number without once picturing a day lived with it.

He set the phone face down. The listing's address remained in his head.

choices.text: Looked at the 2.5 billion one — if going once, go right.
choices.result_text:
If it was going to happen once, do it properly. He enlarged the floor plan of the 2.5-billion listing.

His finger stopped over one room. Once, he would have imagined it as Father's room when he came to Seoul. Father could not come now. Nor could he immediately fill the blank with someone else's name.

Three billion won. Beneath the target written once more, the shape of a home appeared alongside one room he would leave empty.

title: 3 AM
description:
3 AM. Sleep would not come.

A folded medicine packet lay at one side of the desk. Father was younger in the photograph than he had sounded on their last call. Minjun kept his eyes on the calculator so he would not look at the empty chair.

There had been a clear reason at first. Father's guarantee fraud. Six years. After paying off that debt, he needed to build something of his own. Three billion won had been the symbol.

But if he was still chasing the same number now that Father was gone, who was he trying to show it to? At 3 AM he could not tell grief from exhaustion, or either one from having forgotten how to stop.

choices.text: Pulled out the original reason. Not to forget.
choices.result_text:
{name} pulled the notebook from beneath the calculator and opened its first page. The sentence written after the final repayment was more crooked than the figures, and the corners of the paper had worn smooth under years of handling.

Father. Six years. A guarantee that put someone else's debt under Father's own name. Reading the three again did not tell him whether he felt anger or resolve. So instead of naming the feeling, he wrote down one calculation to verify tomorrow and one block of time to clear for his body.

Restoring the goal to its old place did not erase the costs already paid. Beneath three billion won, {name} wrote, "Do not forget why this began," then drew a line to make sure that sentence could not excuse the people he had missed.

When he switched off the calculator, the room went dark. Certainty had not returned. But he knew what he would carry when he stood again.

choices.text: Don't know. Decided to think about it tomorrow.
choices.result_text:
{name} wrote no answer. Instead, he captured the screen with the calculation and question visible together, then set the phone facedown. He would not disguise not knowing as a conclusion.

He left the notebook open beside the calculator. If the question vanished when he saw the same figures in daylight, it had been exhaustion. If it remained, it belonged to the day as well. His 3 a.m. self would decide neither in advance.

He set the alarm later and drank a glass of water. The figures stayed against the back of his eyelids for a while, but this time he did not build a new plan to push sleep away.

The fact that he had deferred the answer remained on the paper. {name} did not call that a solution. Then he slept.

choices.text: For the first time, opened the door to: maybe three billion isn't required.
choices.result_text:
{name} drew a vertical line in the notebook. On the left he wrote THREE BILLION WON. On the right: WHAT MUST STILL REMAIN AFTERWARD. As he began filling the second column, time withheld from his body and promises that had closed came first.

The thought was not as frightening as expected. He had not erased the target or abandoned Gangnam. He had only taken away the figure's authority to make every choice beneath it correct.

{name} crossed out the word MUST and left three billion won untouched. The goal became slightly smaller. The shape of the person who might reach it became more concrete.

Before the sky brightened, he closed the calculator. A door had opened between the size of an account and the value of a life. He chose not to close it yet.

description_if_known.daytime_conviction:
3 AM. Couldn't sleep.

A strange thought surfaced. Does Gangnam actually have to happen?

In the beginning, there was a clear reason. Father's guarantee fraud. Six years. After paying off that debt — needed to build something of your own. Three billion was the symbol of that.

But sometimes, three billion looks like just a number now. Whether this is fatigue, maturity, or surrender — couldn't tell.

Once before, he had carried a 3 a.m. Conviction into daylight to test it.
It held in daylight too.
That memory is a backrest now, against tonight's 3 a.m. Doubt.

description_memory_if_known.arc_y4_midpoint_receipt_seen:
Eleven weeks had passed since he locked the three lines. Beside the calculator lay the long strip he had tucked into the notebook's first page that night. Completion times, dates that would not reopen, and blanks left by his body and family shared the same blue light as the distance remaining to three billion won.

{name} looked once at the number still to go, then once at the three lines already paid. The calculator told him how much farther he had to travel. The paper told him what he had left behind. Tonight's doubt was not a sentence passing through fatigue. It was the question that remained even after he read the ledger he had locked with his own hand.
